block.txt: Where the Registrar-General supplies information in response to a written inquiry as to the manner in which a proposed dealing or plan should be drawn, or whether a proposed dealing or plan should be entitled to registration, by or under this or any other Act—
the Registrar-General may require payment of a prescribed fee, or may supply the information without fee, and
the fact that any such information has been so supplied shall not, of itself, bind the Registrar-General to register or otherwise give effect to any dealing or plan, or any class of dealing or plan.
A regulation prescribing a fee for the purposes of paragraph (a) of subsection (2) may—
prescribe the fee to be paid in the circumstances specified in the regulation,
require, in the circumstances specified in the regulation, the payment of a fee calculated on such basis as may be prescribed by the regulation, or
authorise the Registrar-General to charge, in circumstances not provided for under paragraph (a) or (b), a reasonable fee.

The Registrar-General may reject, or refuse to accept or to take any action in relation to, any primary application, dealing, caveat or priority notice unless it is certified as required by the conveyancing rules.

The Registrar-General may reject, or refuse to accept or to take any action in relation to, any dealing accompanied by a notice under section 39(1B) unless it is certified as required by the conveyancing rules.
A person must not falsely or negligently certify to the correctness of any application, dealing, caveat or notice referred to in this section.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.

The conviction of a person under subsection (4) does not prevent a person who may have sustained any damage or loss in consequence of an error or mistake in any such certified application, dealing or caveat from recovering damages against the person certifying.
The Registrar-General may by written notice (a requisition) given to a person require the person—
to re-execute, complete or correct a dealing, application, request or caveat that has been lodged for registration or recording, or

to provide the Registrar-General with specified information, or produce a specified instrument or other document, in support of a dealing, application, request or caveat that has been lodged for registration or recording.
The regulations may prescribe a fee that is to be paid by the person to whom a requisition is given.
The Registrar-General may refuse to deal with the dealing, application, request or caveat until the requisition has been complied with and the prescribed fee has been paid.

If a requisition in respect of a dealing is complied with, failure to pay the prescribed fee for the requisition does not prevent the dealing from being in registrable form for the purposes of determining the order in which dealings were lodged in registrable form.

heading.b: Proceedings for the possession or recovery of land

heading.b: Registered proprietor protected except in certain cases

block.txt: Proceedings for the possession or recovery of land do not lie against the registered proprietor of the land, except as follows—
proceedings brought by a mortgagee against a mortgagor in default,
proceedings brought by a chargee or covenant chargee against a charger or covenant charger in default,
proceedings brought by a lessor against a lessee in default,
proceedings brought by a person deprived of land by fraud against—
a person who has been registered as proprietor of the land through fraud, or
a person deriving (otherwise than as a transferee bona fide for valuable consideration) from or through a person registered as proprietor of the land through fraud,

proceedings brought by a person deprived of, or claiming, land that (by reason of the misdescription of other land or its boundaries) has been included in a folio of the Register for the other land against a person who has been registered as proprietor of the other land (otherwise than as a transferee bona fide for valuable consideration),

proceedings brought by a registered proprietor under an earlier folio of the Register against a registered proprietor under a later folio of the Register where the two folios have been created for the same land.
Despite any rule of law or equity to the contrary—

the production of a manual folio is an absolute bar and estoppel to any such proceedings commenced before the production of the folio against the person named in the folio as a registered proprietor or lessee of the land, and

the production of a computer folio certificate for a computer folio is an absolute bar and estoppel to any such proceedings commenced before the time specified in the certificate against the person named in the certificate as a registered proprietor or lessee of the land.
Subsection (2) does not apply to proceedings of the kind referred to in subsection (1) (a)–(f).
This section does not affect—
any proceedings in relation to land for which a qualified folio of the Register has been created, being proceedings based on a subsisting interest within the meaning of Part 4A, or

any proceedings brought by a person deprived of, or claiming, land that (by reason of the misdescription of other land or its boundaries) has been included in a limited folio of the Register for the other land, whether or not the registered proprietor of the other land is a transferee of the land bona fide for valuable consideration.

heading.b: Defendant’s entitlements where improvements have been made

block.txt: This section applies to proceedings for the possession or recovery of land in the circumstances referred to in section 118 (1) (e) or (f).
If the defendant or any person through whom the defendant claims has made improvements to the land before the proceedings are commenced—
the fact that the improvements have been made may be pleaded by the defendant, and
if the plaintiff’s title to the land is established—
the value of the improvements, and
the value of the land without the improvements,
are to be separately assessed.

An order for the possession or recovery of the land is not to be made until an amount equivalent to the value of the improvements, less the plaintiff’s costs in the proceedings, is paid into court for payment to the defendant.
If that amount is not paid within 3 months after the assessment is made—
the plaintiff ceases to be entitled to possession of the land and becomes entitled only to an amount equivalent to the sum of—
the value of the land without the improvements, and
the plaintiff’s costs in the proceedings, and
on paying that amount to the plaintiff, the defendant becomes entitled to retain possession of the land.

content.txt: pt 13, div 2, hdg: Ins 2000 No 28, Sch 1 [12].

block.txt: Any person who suffers loss or damage as a result of the operation of this Act in respect of any land, where the loss or damage arises from—
fraud, or
any error, misdescription or omission in the Register, or
the land being brought under the provisions of this Act, or
the registration (otherwise than under section 45E) of some other person as proprietor of the land, estate or interest,
may commence proceedings in the Supreme Court for the recovery of damages.
Such proceedings may be taken only—
against the person whose acts or omissions have given rise to the loss or damage referred to in subsection (1), or
against the Registrar-General.
Proceedings against the Registrar-General are to be taken in accordance with Part 14.

Proceedings cannot be taken under this section against the authorised operator. Proceedings for an act or omission of the authorised operator can instead be taken against the Registrar-General. See section 15 (Liability of authorised operator for compensation) of the Land and Property Information NSW (Authorised Transaction) Act 2016.

heading.b: Administrative review of decisions of Registrar-General

block.txt: A person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar-General made in the exercise of a titling and registry function may apply to the Registrar-General for the decision to be reviewed by the Registrar-General under this section.
Titling and registry functions include functions in respect of land that are exercised by the Registrar-General under the Conveyancing Act 1919 or any other Act.

This section extends to the review of a decision of the Registrar-General that is a decision made by the authorised operator and the Registrar-General is entitled to exercise any function exercisable by the authorised operator in making the decision being reviewed even if the delegation of that function to the authorised operator does not permit the Registrar-General to exercise the function.

The Registrar-General may give notice of a review under this section to any person who in the Registrar-General’s opinion may be affected by the outcome of the review (a notified person), and a notified person is entitled to submit material for the consideration of the Registrar-General on the review.

On the review of a decision under this section, the Registrar-General is to consider any relevant material submitted by the applicant or a notified person within the time allowed by the Registrar-General and may either affirm the decision or vary the decision by setting it aside and making a decision in substitution for the decision that is set aside.
If a decision made by the authorised operator is varied on review, the varied decision is to be given effect to by the authorised operator.

As soon as practicable after a review is finalised the Registrar-General must notify the applicant, each notified person who submitted material for consideration and (where appropriate) the authorised operator of the decision on the review and the reasons for the decision.
A review under this section is taken to be finalised when—
the applicant is notified by the Registrar-General of the decision on the review, or

the applicant is not notified of the decision on the review within 42 days after the application for the review is lodged (or such other period as the Registrar-General and the applicant may agree on).
The regulations may make provision for or with respect to a review under this section, including (without limitation) for or with respect to any of the following—
the time within which an application for review may be made,
the fee to accompany an application for review,
the information required to accompany an application for review,
excluding any class of decisions from the operation of this section.
A review under this section does not affect any right that a person may have to take proceedings against the Registrar-General.

heading.b: Review of decisions by Supreme Court

block.txt: A person who is dissatisfied with the result of the review under section 121 of a decision of the Registrar-General (including a decision made by the authorised operator) may apply to the Supreme Court for a review of the decision.
For the purpose of conducting such a review, the Supreme Court may reconsider and determine any question of fact involved in the decision.
The Registrar-General may not rely on any grounds that are not set out in the reasons given on the review of the decision under section 121 except by leave of the Supreme Court.
After reviewing the Registrar-General’s decision on an application under this section, the Supreme Court—
may uphold the decision, or

may order that the Registrar-General take such action in relation to the matters raised by the application as the Supreme Court considers appropriate, being action that the Registrar-General could, but for the order, have taken,
and may make such further or other orders as the Supreme Court considers appropriate.
This section does not apply to the determination of the position of a boundary under Part 14A.

heading.b: Applicant may state case for Supreme Court

block.txt: If the Registrar-General makes any objection to the title of land the subject of—
an application to bring the land under the provisions of this Act, or
a possessory application,
being an objection that the applicant considers not well founded, the applicant may state a case for the opinion of the Supreme Court.
The Registrar-General is entitled to appear and be heard, either personally or by a legal practitioner, at the hearing of the matter.
The Supreme Court’s opinion on the stated case binds the Registrar-General in relation to the application, but does not affect—
the right conferred on any person by Part 14 to make a claim against the Torrens Assurance Fund, or
the right conferred on the applicant by section 122 to apply for a review of the Registrar-General’s decision on the application.

heading.b: Application to Supreme Court for directions

block.txt: If any question arises concerning the performance or exercise of any duties or functions conferred or imposed on the Registrar-General by or under this or any other Act in respect of any land, the Registrar-General may apply to the Supreme Court for directions on the matter.

The Registrar-General is to give notice of an application under this section to each person who has a registered estate or interest in the land concerned and any other person that the Court directs be given notice of the application. A person who is given notice is entitled to appear and be heard on the application.
The Registrar-General is to give effect to any directions of the Court on an application under this section.

heading.b: Registrar-General may intervene in certain proceedings

block.txt: The Registrar-General may intervene in any proceedings before any court (other than criminal proceedings) if of the opinion that the court’s decision in the proceedings could result in compensation becoming payable from the Torrens Assurance Fund.
The Registrar-General has a right to appear and be heard, either personally or by a legal practitioner, when intervening in any such proceedings.
On intervening in any such proceedings, the Registrar-General becomes a party to the proceedings and has all the rights of such a party.

heading.b: Barring of actions where claimant on notice

block.txt: Proceedings based on a claim of deprivation of land through the bringing of that land under the provisions of this Act do not lie against the Registrar-General where the person alleging the deprivation, or the person through whom he or she claims title—
had notice (by personal service or otherwise) or was otherwise aware that application had been made to bring the land under the provisions of this Act, and
had omitted to lodge a caveat forbidding the bringing of the land under the provisions of this Act or had allowed such a caveat to lapse.

Proceedings based on a claim of deprivation of land through the grant of a possessory application do not lie against the Registrar-General where the person alleging the deprivation, or the person through whom he or she claims title—
had notice (by personal service or otherwise) or was otherwise aware that the application had been made, and
had omitted to lodge a caveat forbidding the grant of the application or had allowed such a caveat to lapse.
Proceedings based on the extinguishment of a restrictive covenant do not lie against the Registrar-General where the person alleging loss from that extinguishment—
had notice (by personal service or otherwise) or was otherwise aware that an application for extinguishment of the restrictive covenant had been made, and
had omitted to lodge a caveat forbidding the grant of the application or had allowed such a caveat to lapse.

Proceedings based on the abandonment of an easement do not lie against the Registrar-General where the person alleging loss from that abandonment, or any previous registered proprietor of the land benefited by that easement—
had notice (by personal service or otherwise) or was otherwise aware that the Registrar-General intended to cancel a recording relating to the easement in the Register, and
had omitted to lodge a caveat forbidding the grant of the application or had allowed such a caveat to lapse.
Proceedings based on the correction of the Register in accordance with this Act by the Registrar-General do not lie against the Registrar-General where the person alleging loss from that correction—
had notice (by personal service or otherwise) or was otherwise aware that the Registrar-General intended to correct the Register, and
had failed to serve on the Registrar-General or give the Registrar-General written notice of an order made by the Supreme Court restraining the action.

administrative proceedings means proceedings on a claim referred to in section 131.
compensable loss means loss or damage of the kind referred to in section 129 (1), other than loss or damage of the kind referred to in section 129 (2).
compensation means compensation from the Torrens Assurance Fund to which a person is entitled under section 129.
court proceedings means proceedings referred to in section 132.
insurer means a professional indemnity insurer and any other person who carries on an insurance business within the meaning of the Insurance Act 1973 of the Commonwealth.

professional indemnity insurer means an insurer, scheme or fund (whether or not established by or under any Act or law) by or from which claims are payable, being claims made by persons sustaining loss or damage owing to any fraudulent, wilful or negligent act or omission by a person carrying on business in a particular profession, trade or calling.
In this Part, approved determination of native title, native title and native title rights and interests have the same meanings as they have in the Native Title Act 1993 of the Commonwealth.

block.txt: Any person who suffers loss or damage as a result of the operation of this Act in respect of any land, where the loss or damage arises from—

any act or omission of the Registrar-General in the execution or performance of his or her functions or duties under this Act in relation to the land (including any such act or omission of the authorised operator), or
the registration (otherwise than under section 45E) of some other person as proprietor of the land, or of any estate or interest in the land, or
any error, misdescription or omission in the Register in relation to the land, or
the land having been brought under the provisions of this Act, or
the person having been deprived of the land, or of any estate or interest in the land, as a consequence of fraud, or
an error or omission in a computer folio certificate or a certificate issued under section 96A in relation to the land, or
any error of the Registrar-General in recording details supplied in the notice referred to in section 39 (1B),
is entitled to payment of compensation from the Torrens Assurance Fund.
Compensation is not payable in relation to any loss or damage suffered by any person—
to the extent to which the loss or damage is a consequence of any act or omission by that person, or
to the extent to which the loss or damage—
is a consequence of any fraudulent, wilful or negligent act or omission by any solicitor, licensed conveyancer, real estate agent or information broker, and
is compensable under an indemnity given by a professional indemnity insurer, or
to the extent to which that person has failed to mitigate the loss or damage, or

to the extent to which the loss or damage has been offset by some other benefit to that person that has arisen from substantially the same circumstances as those from which the loss or damage has arisen, or
where the loss or damage arises because of an error or miscalculation in the measurement of land, or
where the loss or damage arises from—
the breach by a registered proprietor of any trust (whether express, implied or constructive), or
the inclusion of the same land in two or more grants, or

where the loss or damage arises from the recording, or the omitting to record, in the Register of an approved determination of native title or other matter relating to native title rights and interests, or
where the loss or damage arises from circumstances in respect of which this Act provides that proceedings against the Registrar-General do not lie, or
where the loss or damage arises from an error contained in a plan lodged in accordance with Division 3C of Part 2 of the Conveyancing Act 1919, or

where the loss or damage arises from the person’s failure, as mortgagee or transferee of a mortgage, to comply with section 56C or from the cancellation of a recording with respect to a mortgage in accordance with section 56C (6), or
where the loss or damage arises from the recording of a Registrar-General’s caveat in the Register under section 12 (1) (e) or (f) or the removal of such a caveat by the Registrar-General, or

where the loss or damage arises from the execution of an instrument by an attorney (under a power of attorney) acting contrary to, or outside of, the authority conferred on him or her by the power of attorney, or
where the loss or damage is the result of an easement not being recorded in the Register (except where the easement is not recorded in the Register due to an error of the Registrar-General), or
where the loss or damage arises from the improper exercise of a power of sale, or
where the loss or damage arises from the operation of section 129 of the Corporations Act 2001 of the Commonwealth, or
where the loss or damage arises from the provision by the Registrar-General of information supplied in the notice referred to in section 39 (1B) (subject to subsection (1) (g)).
Subsection (2) (g) applies whether the loss or damage is alleged to have been suffered—
by a holder of native title or a claimant for native title, or
by a person deprived of land or an estate or interest in land as a result of the making of an approved determination of native title, or
by any other person,
but does not apply to an error made by the Registrar-General in the recording of matter in the Register.

For the purposes of subsection (2) (m), an error of the Registrar-General does not extend to the Registrar-General’s failure, in relation to the creation of a qualified folio of the Register under Part 4A, to make searches or inquiries as to the existence of any easement.
The entitlement to compensation under subsection (1) does not confer any entitlement to compensation for personal injury.

In this section, information broker means a person who has entered into an agreement with the Registrar-General to make information in the Register available in accordance with the conditions determined by the Registrar-General under section 96B (2).

The total compensation that is payable under this Part, in relation to loss or damage suffered by a person as a result of the person being deprived of land or any estate or interest in land, is limited to the market value of the land at the date on which compensation is awarded to that person plus any legal, valuation or other professional costs reasonably incurred by the person in making the claim.

heading.b: Limits on amount recoverable in respect of mortgage obtained by fraud

block.txt: This section applies only in circumstances where—

a claim for compensation is made as a result of the registration of a mortgage and the execution of the mortgage involved, in the opinion of the Registrar-General, fraud against a registered proprietor of the mortgaged land, and
a person would be entitled to compensation under this Part for deprivation of the mortgaged land as a consequence of fraud if the position of that person is not otherwise rectified, and
as a result of the registration of the mortgage, the mortgagee is entitled to exercise a power of sale in respect of the land mortgaged.
Section 129A does not apply in the circumstances in which this section applies.

The total compensation that is payable to a mortgagee is limited to the market value of the land at the date on which compensation is awarded to the mortgagee less the amount secured by any other mortgage affecting the same land (including a mortgage that is registered as a result of fraud) that has, or would have had, more priority.
Subsections (5) and (6)—
apply to limit the interest and costs components of a claim, and
apply despite anything to the contrary in the mortgage (including any associated document).
The rate of interest to be applied in calculating the interest component of a claim on any particular day must not exceed—
if the interest rate specified in the mortgage is no greater than the official cash rate applicable on that day plus 2%—the interest rate specified in the mortgage, or
if the interest rate specified in the mortgage is greater than the official cash rate applicable on that day plus 2%—the official cash rate plus 2%.

The costs component (being the costs incurred by the mortgagee in relation to the mortgage) of a claim is limited to the reasonable costs incurred by the mortgagee in directly protecting the mortgagee’s interest in respect of the land mortgaged.
In this section, official cash rate means the official cash rate specified by the Reserve Bank of Australia.

heading.b: Minister may direct ex gratia payments from Torrens Assurance Fund

block.txt: Despite section 129 (2), the Minister may, on the recommendation of the Registrar-General, direct that compensation is payable in any of the circumstances referred to in that subsection if, in all of the circumstances of the case, the Minister is satisfied that it would be just to do so.
A decision as to whether or not to give a direction under this section is in the absolute discretion of the Minister.
Without limiting subsection (2), nothing in any recommendation of the Registrar-General requires the Minister to give a direction under this section.
A decision by the Minister under this section may not be called into question in any legal proceedings.

heading.b: Administrative proceedings for recovery of compensation

block.txt: A person who has suffered compensable loss may lodge a claim for compensation, in the approved form, with the Registrar-General.
Such a claim may not be made more than 6 years after—
the date on which the act or omission giving rise to the compensable loss occurred, or
if the compensable loss arose after the date on which that act or omission occurred, the date on which the compensable loss arose.
The regulations may make provision for or with respect to the manner in which a claim is to be made and dealt with.
The Registrar-General may determine a claim by making an offer of settlement or by refusing the claim.
Section 135 applies to the settlement, and any offer of settlement, of a claim.
A claimant must co-operate fully with the Registrar-General for the purpose of ensuring that the Registrar-General has sufficient information to be able—
to assess the validity of the claim, and
to assess the claimant’s compensable loss, and
to make an informed offer of compensation.
In particular, a claimant must comply with any reasonable request by the Registrar-General—
to furnish specified information (including information verified by statutory declaration) or to produce specified documents, or
to take specified action to further the claim.

Without limiting subsection (6), the following information is information that is required to enable the Registrar-General to assess the validity of a claim, assess compensable loss and make an informed offer of compensation—
details of any potential claims that the claimant may have against other parties to which the Registrar-General may be subrogated,

details of any proceedings relating to the circumstances which gave rise to the claim (including the outcome of any such proceedings and whether any party to the proceedings has subrogated another person).
In assessing the reasonableness of a request by the Registrar-General, regard is to be had to the following criteria—
the amount of time the claimant needs to comply with the request,
the degree to which the information, document or action requested is relevant to the determination of the claim,
the degree to which the information already available to the Registrar-General should suffice to enable the claim to be properly determined,
the degree to which compliance with the request would impose undue hardship on the claimant,
the degree to which any information sought by the request is the subject of legal professional privilege,
whether any information, document or action the subject of the request is sufficiently specified,
the timing of the request, having regard to its effect on the claimant’s ability to commence court proceedings,
such other criteria as are relevant to the question of whether the request is reasonable.

Without limiting the power of the Registrar-General to refuse a claim in accordance with subsection (4), the Registrar-General may refuse a claim on the ground that a claimant has failed to comply with a request made under subsection (7) if—
the request was made by notice in writing, and
at least 2 months have elapsed since the notice was given to the claimant.

For the purposes of section 132, a claim is taken to have been refused if it is not determined within 12 months after the claim was made. However, if at the end of that period the claimant has failed to provide information in fulfilment of the duty imposed by subsection (6), the claim is only taken to have been refused if it is not determined within 2 months after that information is provided.

Subsection (9) does not prevent a claim from being determined under this section in favour of the claimant after the expiry of the relevant period limited by that subsection, if the claimant has not commenced proceedings under section 132.

Interest at the rate payable on an unpaid judgment of the Supreme Court under the Supreme Court Act 1970 is payable on an offer of compensation that has been accepted by the claimant in administrative proceedings to the extent to which the amount accepted remains unpaid at the end of 28 days after the date on which it was accepted.

heading.b: Court proceedings for the recovery of compensation

block.txt: Proceedings before a court for the payment of compensation are to be taken against the Registrar-General as nominal defendant.
Any such court proceedings may only be commenced—
if administrative proceedings have been commenced and determined in relation to the compensable loss, or
by leave of the court or with the consent of the Registrar-General.

Court proceedings commenced in accordance with subsection (2) (a) must be commenced within 3 months of the date on which the administrative proceedings have been determined in relation to the compensable loss.
Court proceedings may be commenced at any time during the period of 3 months referred to in subsection (2A) despite any provision of the Limitation Act 1969 to the contrary.
In any court proceedings, the Registrar-General is not bound by any prejudicial act or omission by any party to the proceedings, such as—
entering into, or offering to enter into, a compromise, or
granting, or offering to grant, a release or waiver.

If court proceedings are commenced following administrative proceedings that have been determined by the offer of compensation and the compensation awarded by the court (less any interest awarded in relation to the period after the date of the offer) is less than the compensation offered by the determination—
the claimant’s costs in the court proceedings are not payable by the Registrar-General, and
the Registrar-General’s costs are payable by the claimant,
unless the court orders otherwise.
If court proceedings are commenced following the refusal of a claim in accordance with section 131 (8A)—
the claimant’s costs in the court proceedings are not payable by the Registrar-General, and
the Registrar-General’s costs are payable by the claimant, and
the claimant is not entitled to any interest in respect of the amount of compensation claimed from the date of the notice referred to in section 131 (8A),
unless the court orders otherwise.

If court proceedings are commenced with the leave of the court or the consent of the Registrar-General under subsection (2), the claimant must co-operate fully with the Registrar-General for the purpose of ensuring that the Registrar-General has sufficient information to be able—
to assess the validity of the claim, and
to assess the claimant’s compensable loss, and
to make an informed offer of compensation.
If a claimant fails to comply with subsection (7)—
the claimant’s costs in the court proceedings are not payable by the Registrar-General, and
the Registrar-General’s costs are payable by the claimant, and
where the Registrar-General has requested information in accordance with subsection (7) in writing—the claimant is not entitled to any interest on the claim from the date of that notice,
unless the court orders otherwise.

heading.b: Subrogation of rights to claim compensation

block.txt: An insurer cannot be subrogated to any other person in respect of that other person’s right to claim compensation from the Torrens Assurance Fund in relation to compensable loss.

If administrative proceedings or court proceedings are commenced in relation to a claimant’s compensable loss, the Registrar-General is subrogated to the claimant in respect of the claimant’s rights and remedies against any person in relation to that loss.
In the case of a deceased person, the compensation may be recovered from the deceased person’s estate by proceedings taken against the deceased person’s personal representative.

The Registrar-General may join any person in any court proceedings if of the opinion that the claimant has a cause of action against that person in respect of the compensable loss to which the proceedings relate.
This section has effect despite any provision of the Legal Profession Uniform Law (NSW) or any other Act, law or agreement.
If a claimant—
receives a payment from the Torrens Assurance Fund in respect of the claim, and
receives or recovers from another source or sources a payment on account of the compensable loss, and
there is a surplus after deducting the amount of the compensable loss from the total amount received or recovered by the claimant from both or all sources,
the amount of the surplus is a debt payable by the claimant to the Torrens Assurance Fund.
However, the amount payable by the claimant cannot exceed the amount the claimant received from the Torrens Assurance Fund in respect of the claim.
There is established in the Special Deposits Account an account called the Torrens Assurance Fund.
The following amounts are to be paid into the Torrens Assurance Fund—

any amounts that the Minister directs to be paid as contributions to the Fund from or as an addition to fees (lodgment fees) payable to the Registrar-General for lodgment of any dealing, caveat or withdrawal of caveat,
any amounts recovered by the Registrar-General under or in connection with this Part,
any amounts advanced by the Treasurer for payment into the Fund,
any amounts appropriated by Parliament for payment into the Fund,
any amounts required by or under this or any other Act or law to be paid into the Fund.
The following amounts are payable out of the Torrens Assurance Fund—
any compensation payable under or in connection with this Part,
any amounts required to repay any advance made by the Treasurer for payment into the Fund,
any costs and expenses incurred by the Registrar-General in connection with any claim for compensation from the Fund, including the payment of compensation in settlement of any such claim,
any costs and expenses incurred by the Registrar-General in, or as incidental to, the administration of the Fund,
any other amounts required by or under this or any other Act or law to be paid out of the Fund.

For the purpose of the collection of amounts directed to be paid as contributions to the Fund from lodgment fees, those fees may be prescribed so as to include the amount to be contributed. If a contribution is directed to be paid as an addition to a lodgment fee, the amount payable as the lodgment fee is increased by the amount of the required contribution.
Any shortfall in the Torrens Assurance Fund is to be met from the Consolidated Fund, which is appropriated accordingly.
The Torrens Assurance Fund is to repay the Consolidated Fund.
The Registrar-General may settle any claim for payment of compensation from the Torrens Assurance Fund, whether in the course of litigation to enforce the claim or otherwise.
For the purpose of settling such a claim, the Registrar-General may participate in proceedings in the nature of mediation or neutral evaluation.
The power of the Registrar-General to settle such a claim is subject to the following restrictions—
the claim must not be settled unless the Registrar-General is satisfied—
that the claimant would or will be successful in proceedings to enforce the claim, or
that it is otherwise reasonable in all the circumstances of the case to settle the claim,
any amount to be paid in settlement of the claim must not exceed $100,000 (or such other amount as may be prescribed by the regulations) unless the Minister has approved of the settlement.
In settling such a claim, the Registrar-General—
may pay such amount (which may include amounts by way of costs and interest) as the Registrar-General thinks reasonable, and
may, instead of or in addition to payment of a settlement amount, take other action.
A settlement amount may include any costs incurred by the claimant before the settlement.
The Registrar-General may delegate to a member of staff of the Department the power of the Registrar-General to settle claims under this section.
In this Part—
owner, in relation to land, means any person entitled to an estate of freehold in possession in the land—
whether in fee simple or for life or otherwise, and
whether at law or in equity, and
whether absolutely or by way of mortgage.

heading.b: Application may be made for boundary determination

block.txt: Application may be made to the Registrar-General for the determination under this Part of the position of the common boundary of adjoining lands.
Such an application can be made only by or on behalf of—
an owner of land on either side of the boundary, or

the purchaser under a contract for sale of land on one side of the boundary but only if the owner of the land consents to the application or the whole of the purchase price has been paid to the owner or the owner’s agent, or
a public or local authority or the Head of a Government Department.
This Part authorises the determination of the position of a boundary between adjoining parcels of land, whether or not each parcel is under the provisions of this Act.

content.txt: s 135C: Ins 1989 No 171, Sch 1 (2). Subst 1999 No 58, Sch 1 [21].

block.txt: An application for a boundary determination under this Part—
is to be made in a form approved by the Registrar-General, and
is to be accompanied by such information and documents in support of the application as the Registrar-General may require (either generally or in the particular case), and
is to be accompanied by the prescribed application fee.
The Registrar-General must refuse to make the determination unless satisfied, on investigation, that there is doubt as to the position of the boundary concerned.
The Registrar-General is to give notice to an applicant if the Registrar-General refuses to make the determination and is to give reasons for that refusal.

heading.b: Notice of application to be given to certain persons

block.txt: Before determining the position of a boundary pursuant to an application, the Registrar-General is to give notice of the application—
to the owner of each parcel of land adjoining the boundary concerned (other than land owned by the applicant), and
to such other persons as the Registrar-General considers appropriate.

The notice is to contain such details of the application as the Registrar-General considers appropriate and is to invite the person to make a written submission concerning the application within a specified period (not less than 21 days).
In determining the position of the boundary, the Registrar-General is to take into consideration any submissions made in accordance with the requirements of such a notice.
In determining the position of a boundary under this Part, the Registrar-General must consult with a registered land surveyor within the meaning of the Surveying and Spatial Information Act 2002.
If the Registrar-General decides that a survey or other investigation should be carried out to assist the Registrar-General in determining the position of the boundary, the Registrar-General—
may require any applicant for the determination to pay the reasonable costs of any such survey or investigation (and for that purpose may require payment in advance), and
may refuse to proceed with the determination until the required payment is made.

If as a result of considering an application under this Part in respect of a boundary of land, the Registrar-General becomes aware that there is doubt as to the position of another boundary of that or other land, the Registrar-General may determine the position of that other boundary.
Before making a determination under this section, the Registrar-General—

is to give notice of the proposed determination to the owner of each parcel of land adjoining that other boundary inviting the person to make a written submission on the matter within a specified period (not less than 21 days), and
is to take into consideration any submissions made in accordance with the requirements of such a notice.
The Registrar-General must not make a determination under this section without prior consultation with the Surveyor-General.

The Registrar-General is to determine the position of a boundary on the basis of all the evidence available to the Registrar-General but, if that evidence is inconclusive, may determine it on the basis of what appears to the Registrar-General to be just and reasonable in the circumstances.
The Registrar-General is to give notice of a determination of the position of a boundary under this Part—
to any applicant for the determination, and
to the owner of each parcel of land adjoining the boundary, and
to the Surveyor-General, and
to such other persons as the Registrar-General considers appropriate.

heading.b: Appeals to Land and Environment Court

block.txt: A person who is dissatisfied with a determination under this Part may appeal to the Land and Environment Court for determination by the Court of the position of the boundary.
Only the following persons can appeal—
an owner of land adjoining the boundary,
a person who applied for the determination as purchaser under a contract for the sale of land adjoining the boundary,
a public or local authority or the Head of a Government Department.
An appeal must be made not later than 28 days after notice of the Registrar-General’s determination is given to the person concerned.
The appellant must join each owner of land adjoining the boundary (except, in each case, an appellant owner) as a party to the following proceedings—
proceedings on an appeal under this section,
proceedings on any appeal under the Land and Environment Court Act 1979 in respect of the appeal.
The Registrar-General is not to take action under section 135K (Noting of boundary on plans etc)—
until the expiration of the period during which an appeal can be made against the determination concerned to the Land and Environment Court, and
(if an appeal is made during that period) until the matter has been determined by the Land and Environment Court.

The Registrar-General is entitled to be joined as a party, and to appear and be heard either personally or by his or her duly appointed agent, at the hearing of an appeal under this section and at the hearing of any appeal under the Land and Environment Court Act 1979 in respect of any such appeal.

heading.b: Noting of boundary on plans etc

block.txt: When the position of a boundary is determined under this Part, the Registrar-General—

is to make such notations and entries on any plan or other document registered or recorded under this Act or the Conveyancing Act 1919 as may be necessary to show the position of the boundary determined, and
may cause to be so registered a plan showing the position of the boundary determined.
The Registrar-General may also amend any plan or other document to correct any error in it or supply any omission from it in respect of the position of the boundary.
The Registrar-General may also take action under this section in respect of the determination by a competent court of the position of a boundary as if it were a determination under this Part.

The Registrar-General may, if the position of a boundary is determined under this Part, request the applicant for the boundary determination to lodge a plan for registration or recording (being, if the Registrar-General so specifies, a plan of survey) showing details of the boundary as so determined.
The Registrar-General may refuse to take action under this section if an applicant fails to comply with a request under subsection (4).
A determination of the position of a boundary under this Part takes effect when the position of the boundary is shown as referred to in section 135K (1).
Once the determination takes effect, the boundary is for all purposes to be taken to be in the position so shown despite any discrepancy with any plan of survey or other plan or any other record.

The Registrar-General may delegate to any officer or other person employed in the office of the Registrar-General any of the Registrar-General’s powers, authorities, duties or functions under this Part.

A delegate may sub-delegate to any such officer or person any power, authority, duty or function delegated by the Registrar-General if the delegate is authorised in writing to do so by the Registrar-General.

heading.b: Application of provisions where land has more than one owner

block.txt: If land has more than one owner, a notice given to or by one or more of those owners for the purposes of this Part is to be taken to have been given to or by all the owners of the land.

heading.b: Owners may agree to dispense with certain requirements

block.txt: If the owners of all parcels of land adjoining a boundary that is the subject of an application under this Part consent in writing to this section applying, the Registrar-General—
need not comply with the requirements of section 135E (Notice of application to be given to certain persons) in respect of the application, and

may take action under section 135K (Noting of boundary on plans etc) in respect of a determination of the boundary concerned without having regard to section 135J (4) (action delayed to allow appeal to Court).

heading.b: Failure to notify does not affect validity of determination

block.txt: A failure by the Registrar-General to give notice to a person as required by this Part does not affect the validity of any boundary determination with which the requirement to give notice is concerned.
A notice under this part may be given—
for a notice given to the Registrar-General—by leaving the notice at, or sending the notice by pre-paid post to, an office of the Registrar-General, or
otherwise—in the approved way.
Nothing in this section—
affects the operation of any other law of the State that authorises the service of a document in any other way, and
affects the power of a court to authorise service of a document in any other way.

heading.b: Court may direct cancellation of folios and other actions related to folios

block.txt: A court may, in proceedings for the recovery of any land, estate or interest from the person registered as proprietor of the land, make ancillary orders of the kind set out in subsection (3), if the court is of the opinion that the circumstances of the case require any such order to be made.

A court may, in proceedings in which the court makes a determination as to an estate or interest in land, make ancillary orders of the kind set out in subsection (3) if in the court’s opinion the order is needed to give effect to the court’s determination.
A court may order the Registrar-General to do one or more of the following—
cancel or amend a folio of the Register,
cancel, amend or make a recording in a folio of the Register,
create a new folio of the Register,
create a new edition of a computer folio.

If a court makes an order under subsection (3) (c), the Registrar-General may require a person to lodge with the Registrar-General a plan (being, where the Registrar-General so specifies, a plan of survey) of the relevant land, together with such number of copies of the plan, if any, as the Registrar-General may specify.
The Registrar-General must give effect to any such order.
A court that makes an order under this section may order that a person deliver an instrument to the Registrar-General for the purpose of giving effect to any such order.

An action does not lie against the Registrar-General for recovery of damages sustained through deprivation of land, or any estate or interest in land, because of compliance by the Registrar-General with an order under this section.
In this section—
court does not include the Local Court or a tribunal.

heading.b: Registrar-General may take steps to rectify Register in case of fraud

block.txt: The Registrar-General may, in relation to the settlement of a claim in accordance with section 135, take any of the steps set out in subsection (2) that are required to rectify the Register (including by registering a person as proprietor of land) if the Registrar-General is satisfied that—
the person has been deprived of land, or an estate or interest in land, as a result of fraud, and
the current registered proprietor acquired the estate or interest in land through fraud.
The Registrar-General may do one or more of the following—
cancel or amend a folio of the Register,
cancel, amend or make a recording in a folio of the Register,
create a new folio of the Register,
create a new edition of a computer folio,

heading.b: Certain fraudulent acts to be deemed indictable offences

block.txt: If any person—
fraudulently procures, assists in fraudulently procuring or is privy to the fraudulent procuring of—
the creation of a folio of the Register,
a recording in the Register, or
any alteration in any instrument or form issued by the Registrar-General,
fraudulently uses, assists in fraudulently using, or is privy to the fraudulent using of any form purporting to be issued or sanctioned by the Registrar-General, or

knowingly misleads or deceives any person hereinbefore authorised to demand explanation or information in respect to any land or the title to any land which is the subject of any application to bring the same under the provisions of this Act, or in respect to which any dealing is proposed to be registered or recorded,

he or she shall be guilty of an indictable offence, and shall incur a penalty not exceeding 10 penalty units, or may, at the discretion of the Court before whom the case may be tried, be imprisoned for any period not exceeding three years.
Any folio of the Register, recording or alteration the creation or making of which has been procured by fraud shall be void as between all parties or privies to the fraud.

heading.b: Conviction not to affect civil remedy

block.txt: No proceeding or conviction of an indictable offence against this Act shall affect any remedy which any person aggrieved or injured by the offence may be entitled to at law or in equity against the person who has committed the offence or against the estate of the person who has committed the offence.

Except in any case herein otherwise expressly provided, all offences against the provisions of this Act may be prosecuted, and all penalties or sums of money imposed or declared to be due or owing by or under the provisions of the same may be sued for and recovered in the name of the Attorney or Solicitor General before any Court having jurisdiction for punishment of offences of the like nature or for the recovery of penalties or sums of money of the like amount.

The Governor may make regulations not inconsistent with this Act prescribing all such matters as are by this Act required or permitted to be prescribed or as may be necessary or convenient to be prescribed for the administration of this Act and, without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations for or with respect to—
the fees, charges and expenses recoverable by the Registrar-General in the administration of this Act, and
matters for which a fee may be recovered by the Registrar-General, and
the refund or waiver of any such fees, charges or expenses, and
the circumstances in which a plan lodged for registration shall be, or may be required by the Registrar-General to be, a plan of survey.

In subsection (1), a reference to “the administration of this Act” includes a reference to the administration of any other Act in so far as that other Act affects the functions of the Registrar-General with respect to land under the provisions of this Act, whether or not that other Act makes provision for matters to be prescribed thereunder with respect to that land.

The regulations may include provision for or with respect to the increase on an annual or other basis in accordance with a formula prescribed by the regulations of fees, charges and expenses prescribed by the regulations.
A fee, charge or expense can be prescribed by the regulations either as a specified amount or an amount calculated or determined in a specified manner.

heading.b: Fixing of fees etc for new services under relevant Acts

block.txt: A fee, charge or expense that is required or permitted to be prescribed by the regulations under a relevant Act or that is otherwise recoverable by the Registrar-General in the administration of a relevant Act is to be fixed by the Registrar-General (instead of being prescribed by regulations under the relevant Act) if it is recoverable for or in respect of a new titling and registry service.

A new titling and registry service is a titling and registry service for which a fee was not prescribed by regulations under a relevant Act immediately before completion of the authorised asset transfer under the Land and Property Information NSW (Authorised Transaction) Act 2016.
The regulations under a relevant Act may include provision for or with respect to limiting any increase in a fee, charge or expense fixed by the Registrar-General under this section.
A fee, charge or expense fixed by the Registrar-General may be waived or refunded in circumstances determined by the Registrar-General.

A provision of a relevant Act as to the circumstances or manner in which a fee, charge or expense is authorised or required to be prescribed by regulations under the Act extends to a fee, charge or expense fixed by the Registrar-General under this section.

A reference in a relevant Act (however expressed) to a fee, charge or expense prescribed by the regulations includes a reference to a fee, charge or expense fixed by the Registrar-General under this section.
In this section, relevant Act means each of the following Acts—
this Act,
the Conveyancing Act 1919,
the Strata Schemes Development Act 2015,
any other Act prescribed for the purposes of this section by the regulations under this Act.
Schedule 3 has effect.

An act or omission by the Registrar-General, or by any person acting under the direction, or with the authority, of the Registrar-General, does not subject the Registrar-General or any person so acting personally to any action, liability, claim or demand if the act or omission was done or omitted to be done in good faith in the administration or execution of this Act.

heading.b: Cessation of issue of certificates of title

block.txt: The Registrar-General may, by order published in the Gazette, declare that the Registrar-General will cease to issue certificates of title under this Act on a specified day (the cessation day).
The cessation day must be no earlier than the first day after the end of the period of 3 months, beginning with the day on which the order referred to in subclause (1) is published in the Gazette.
On and from the cessation day—
the Registrar-General is no longer required to issue certificates of title under this Act or any other Act, and

a certificate of title previously issued has no force or effect for the purposes of a requirement, whether made under this Act or any other Act, for the lodgment or production of a certificate of title that is imposed in connection with the registration of a matter.
This clause applies to a dealing that—
is lodged with the Registrar-General before the cessation day, and
is not registered by the cessation day, and
at the time of lodgment required a certificate of title for registration.
A dealing to which this clause applies is to be dealt with under the requirements that applied when the dealing was lodged with the Registrar-General.
If a dealing is withdrawn and relodged—
subclause (2) does not apply, and
the dealing is to be dealt with under the requirements that apply when it is relodged.
Subject to the State Records Act 1998, the Registrar-General may—
destroy a paper document that the Registrar-General is not under a duty to deliver or issue to a person, whether or not it is part of the Register, or
deliver a paper document that the Registrar-General is empowered to destroy under paragraph (a) to a person who, in the Registrar-General’s opinion, intends to preserve it for historical purposes.
Before destroying a document under subclause (1)(a) the Registrar-General must make a reproducible copy of the document if—
for a document that is part of the Register—it evidences a subsisting interest, or
for a document that is not part of the Register—the Registrar-General would, but for subclause (1)(a), have a duty to preserve it.

The Registrar-General must preserve a reproducible copy of a document referred to in subclause (2)(a) or (b) for as long as the interest evidenced by the document subsists or for as long as the Registrar-General would, but for subclause (1)(a), have had a duty to preserve the document.

If a reproducible copy of a document is preserved under subclause (3) and that document would, if it had not been destroyed under subclause (1)(a), be part of the Register, whether for all purposes or for the purpose only of section 96B, the reproducible copy is part of the Register for all purposes or for that purpose.
In this clause—
reproducible copy means a copy of a document that is captured and kept in a way that enables the document to be reproduced.
The repeal of section 46B of this Act by the amending Act has no effect on any title to land that had previously been validated by that section.
The repeal of section 46C(4) of this Act by the amending Act has no effect on—
the validity of any recording in the Register that was deemed by that section to have been authorised, or
the validity of the issue of any certificate of title that was deemed by that section to have been validly issued.
